name: Tara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Northgate Design, a studio of five on the high street, above a dentist. We do menus, shopfront signs and branding for restaurants and local shops. A normal day is a menu redesign in the morning, because some café has changed its prices again, and then logo sketches in the afternoon. Every couple of weeks I go out with Simon, the owner, to measure up a shopfront for a new sign.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing my sign go up on a real street. There's a bakery on Elm Road with my lettering on the window, and I walk past it to get the bus. What wears me out is menus, honestly, the endless price changes. I use an AI tool now and then to cut out food photos, but only since Simon started doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, and get on with it. At work I'd say it's nice the background removal stays, since that's useful. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't post opinions much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. I'm not great yet, Simon tells me my kerning is wonky, so time to improve is good. And I've got my flat, which my parents helped me buy, so money feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate and ask Simon to let me do one full brand a quarter, not just menus. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month, maybe a hundred extra. And I'd do a weekend lettering workshop to fix the wonky kerning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things would be steady, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The menu updates are fairly routine. Would AI taking those bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at all. If software updates the café's prices on the menus, I'd cheer. I'd just need Simon to give me something better to do with that time, and I think he would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any other pressures in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage rate resets in two years, which could add a bit. And I'm on my own, so it's one income. But I've got more than six months saved, so I'm not losing sleep.

say: I'd say **that's that**, and get on with things.
At work I'd say keeping **background removal** is useful, and online I'd stay quiet.
think: I'm **relieved**, because my kerning still needs work.
My **flat**, bought with my parents' help, makes money feel **okay**.
do: Ask the owner for **one full brand** each quarter.
Overpay the **mortgage** by about a hundred a month.

fieldNote: She's **happy to lose** routine menu updates to software.
A **single income** and a mortgage reset are her only quiet pressures.
Her parents' **help with the flat** underpins her calm.

steps.text: Ask Simon to let her lead one full brand each quarter
Overpay the mortgage by about a hundred each month
Take a weekend lettering workshop to fix her kerning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and we'd better be sensible about it. At work I'd say let's learn the tools that clearly work and ignore the rest. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the studio would hire fewer people like me. A lot of my day is menus and resizing, which is exactly the thinking work AI takes. Simon would keep me if he could, but he watches costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what other studios on the high street do for a few months. Once a couple of them were using the AI tools for menus, I'd learn them properly myself. I'd ask Simon if I could go out to more client meetings, so I'm the friendly face, not just the hands. And I'd build my savings up to a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My job could shrink or go part-time, and I'm on one income with a mortgage. But I still feel I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to learn the tools. What if waiting costs you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it would. But I've seen colleagues spend weeks on things that went nowhere. I'd wait months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why client meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because café owners like talking to a person. When Mrs Okafor (the bakery owner) wanted her window lettering, she wanted someone to stand outside with her and squint at it. Software can't squint at a shop window with a café owner.

At work I'd say learn tools that **clearly work** and ignore the rest.
think: I expect the studio to **hire fewer** juniors like me.
Menus and **resizing**, most of my day, are what AI takes.
do: Watch other **high street studios** for a few months.
Learn the **AI tools** once a couple of studios use them.
Ask for more **client meetings** and build savings to **a year**.
feel: **Anxious**, on one income with a **mortgage**, but able to steer.

steps.text: Watch what other high street studios do for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened too fast for anyone, and the government needs to help people cover their homes. At work I'd ask Simon straight out what he's planning. Online, still quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my design work is mostly gone by 2028. The bit that lasts longer is measuring up shopfronts and fitting signs, and that's maybe a tenth of my week. It's not enough to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd ask Simon if I could move into fitting signs with the installer he uses, Vic. I'd rent out my flat and move into my parents' spare room to cover the mortgage. I'd learn the AI tools fast too, because in two years they'd be the only way to keep any design work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep over the flat. It's the one thing I've built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years before robots mean for your sign fitting plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're three years of ladders and drills before a robot can do it, around 2031. It's not long, but it pays the mortgage while I work out what next. Maybe by then there'd be some scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would moving back to your parents feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, embarrassing. But my parents would be glad, mum's been asking me to visit more anyway. My flat is the one thing I've built, and keeping the flat matters more than my pride.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone, and ask my boss what he plans.
I'd ask the **government** to help people **keep their homes**.
think: My **design work** is mostly gone by 2028.
Sign fitting is only **a tenth** of my week, not enough to live on.
do: Ask to move into **sign fitting** with the studio's installer.
**Rent out** my flat and move into my parents' spare room.
Learn the **AI tools** fast to keep some design work.
S2.quote: My flat is the one thing I've built, and keeping the flat matters more than my pride.
fieldNote: Under speed she drops her **wait-and-see** habit.
She sees sign fitting as **three paid years** before robots arrive around 2031.

steps.text: Ask Simon to let her fit signs with Vic the installer
Rent out the flat to cover the mortgage
Move into her parents' spare room
Learn the AI design tools quickly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if people start now. At work I'd suggest we sit down and plan. I'd still not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the design job still goes by 2031, but five years lets me pay down the mortgage a lot. That's my real plan: be close to owning the flat outright when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a lot more into the mortgage, maybe four hundred a month. I'd learn the AI tools in the next year, once Simon's used them for a while. I'd take on more of the sign fitting with Vic, aiming for half my week by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a grip on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2034, when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe I'd be doing something with people, like running the shop side of a print place. With the flat mostly paid off, I could take lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a lot of sacrifice for five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's less going out and no big holiday. I'd rather skip the holiday in Portugal than lose my flat.

think: My real plan is to be **near owning** the flat when it hits.

Learn the **AI tools** within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're sensible. At work I'd say let's take it step by step. I'd say the same to my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel I had time to build something. The design job goes by 2036, but I'd be 37, with the flat nearly paid. It's not a disaster, it's a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate five years and learn the tools as Simon brings them in. I'd do a part-time course in project management, so I could run sign and shopfit jobs. And I'd keep overpaying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. Mostly I'd feel like I can handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Project management is thinking work too. Doesn't AGI take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But running a shopfit means being on site, dealing with builders and shop owners. I think that lasts until the robots come too, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone starting a design diploma now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell anyone starting a design diploma to learn a hands-on skill alongside it, like sign-making. And to buy somewhere small if they can, because rent eats you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit before I've paid much off the flat. What would help is a pause on mortgage payments for people losing work, or help to cover them for a year while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about living alone. If you're on your own, there's no second income to fall back on. That changes how you see all of this.

headlineQuote: If you're on your own, there's no second income to fall back on.
portrait: Tara is a **junior designer** making menus and shop signs at a five-person studio.
She lives **alone** in a flat bought with her **parents' help**.
She adopts AI tools **once proven** locally, and values steady, sensible change.
Her plans revolve around **protecting the flat** and moving into sign fitting.
She's **calm** in a plateau and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would hit before she's paid much off the flat.
whatWouldHelp: A year of **mortgage support** for people losing work while they retrain.
